title: Gaulish
description: The month names of the Coligny calendar, the only long record of a Celtic calendar
origin: The names come from the Coligny calendar, a bronze tablet of about the 2nd century AD found in eastern France in 1897. It records a lunisolar calendar in Gaulish, with 12 lunar months in a year and an extra month added about every two and a half years. Scholars have reconstructed the names and proposed meanings, but the tablet gives no seasons, so where each month fell in the solar year is a choice. Here Cantlos comes first and Samonios sits in slot 3, which is one of several placements scholars have argued for.
pronunciation: A scholarly reconstruction: Latin letters are read as in Latin, with each vowel said separately and w for u or v between vowels. Gaulish is known only from inscriptions like this tablet, so the sounds are a best guess, and the stress is the least certain part. Stress marks follow the usual Celtic pattern of stressing the syllable before the ending, but nobody knows for sure.

leapWeek.name: Leap week
leapWeek.meaning: The Coligny calendar kept the moon and sun in step by adding a whole leap month about every two and a half years. This calendar adds a week instead, at the end of the year, about one year in six.

months.name: Cantlos
months.meaning: The last month of the Coligny year. Xavier Delamarre suggests month of chanting, and Mary Jones's table has song. Both are guesses.

months.name: Quimonios
months.meaning: The tablet's first leap month, placed before Samonios. Its name is only partly preserved, as QVIMON, and its meaning is unknown.
months.notes: The 13th month. Quimonios is a reconstructed name for the first of the calendar's two leap months. The second is only partly legible.

months.name: Samonios
months.meaning: Delamarre and Matasovic derive it from a Proto-Celtic word for an assembly or feast, perhaps of the living and the dead. Linking it to Gaulish samo, summer, is probably a folk etymology.
months.notes: Where Samonios fell in the solar year is unresolved. Some scholars tie it to the start of winter, near Samhain, and others to early summer, so slot 3 is a choice, not a fact.

months.name: Dumannios
months.meaning: Delamarre suggests month of fumigations, linking it to Latin fumus, smoke.

months.name: Rivros
months.meaning: Delamarre suggests fat month, comparing Old Irish remor and Welsh rhef, thick or stout. Mary Jones gives frost instead. Both are scholarly guesses.

months.name: Anagantios
months.meaning: Read in several ways: the month in which one does not travel, a month of protection, or a month of ritual washing. Scholars have not settled between them.

months.name: Ogronios
months.meaning: Delamarre suggests month of cold or winter. The meaning is a guess from related words.

months.name: Cutios
months.meaning: Delamarre suggests month of invocations. It is a scholarly guess.

months.name: Giamonios
months.meaning: Made from the Gaulish word for winter, giamos, which matches Old Irish gam and Welsh gaeaf. The etymology is transparent. Samonios and Giamonios are often taken to open the summer and winter halves of the year.

months.name: Simiuisonnios
months.meaning: Possibly half of the sun's course, or half-spring, from simi, half. The second part of the name is debated.

months.name: Equos
months.meaning: Possibly a month of horses or livestock, from the Gaulish word for horse. It is the month that could have 29 or 30 days.

months.name: Elembiuios
months.meaning: Delamarre reads it as the month of the stag. The reading is plausible, but the name is only partly understood.

months.name: Edrinios
months.meaning: Possibly linked to Old Irish aed, fire or heat, which would make it a month of heat. It is a guess.
